sections.html:
Hilton Head Island is a barrier island in Beaufort County, in the Lowcountry about 20 miles northeast of Savannah. The Town counted 37,661 residents in 2020, and 40.3% of its 29,018 housing units are vacant, which reflects the many second homes and rentals. The median value of an owner-occupied home was $687,400 for 2020 to 2024.

Owners often live elsewhere, so a sale that does not require flying in for open houses has real appeal. Everything here is shaped by the island setting: the bridge, the tides, the gates and the water. About 70% of the island, including most resort areas, lies inside gated communities. Sea Pines Resort, Hilton Head Plantation, Palmetto Dunes, Shipyard Plantation and Port Royal Plantation are the best known. Each has its own association and rules, so learn them before any sale.

sections.h2: Flood zones and records to gather
sections.html:
Flood zone status comes up in nearly every sale. The Town publishes a Flood Hazard Zone Search, and its guide defines the zones below.

Flood zoneWhat it means
Zone XLow risk
Shaded Zone X0.2% annual chance of flooding
Zone AE1% annual chance
Zone VE1% annual chance, with wave action
Zone AOShallow flooding

The Town is a Class 5 community in FEMA's Community Rating System and has taken part since 1991, which it says gives property owners a 25% discount on flood insurance premiums. Summers are humid, with a July average high of 90 degrees and about 51.4 inches of rain a year, and August is the wettest month at 8.9 inches.

Before you sell, gather:

  • A current elevation certificate, which the Floodplain Administrator can help with
  • Building permit history, which the Town lets you search by address
  • Your flood insurance declarations page

Permits for buildings from after April 2014, from 1984 to April 2014, and from before 1984 each sit in a different system, and the oldest are requested from Beaufort County. Call the Floodplain Administrator at 843-341-4600 with zone questions.

A house used for vacation rentals needs a Town permit and a business license. The permit is issued to an individual, not a business entity, and the permit number must appear in every advertisement.

Other requirements include an HOA approval letter where one applies, a site plan showing trash and parking, an owner or agent who can be reached during each rental with a one hour complaint response, and the 3% Local Accommodations Tax. Houses of 3,600 square feet or more need a fire suppression or approved monitoring system, and bedrooms must meet code and be primarily for sleeping.

Before you tell a buyer the rental income comes with the house, call the STR office at 843-341-4740 or write STRPlan@hiltonheadislandsc.gov to ask how the permit is handled at a sale.

Hilton Head Island owners pay property tax to Beaufort County, and the gap between the 4% and 6% assessment ratio can be large. South Carolina assesses an owner-occupied legal residence at 4% and other real property, including second homes, at 6%.

The county's application for the 4% rate is due by January 15, and taxes are due by that date whether or not the application is approved. Renting the home for more than 72 days in a calendar year, moving your legal residence or selling must be reported to the Assessor within six months. Keeping the 4% rate improperly brings a penalty of 100% of the tax paid plus 0.5% interest per month, with a $30 minimum. A new owner must submit a fresh application.

State law makes taxes due between September 30 and January 15, with a 3% penalty after January 15, 7% more after February 1 and 5% more after March 16.

sections.h2: Recording a deed in Beaufort County
sections.html:
Deeds for Hilton Head Island go to the Beaufort County Register of Deeds at 100 Ribaut Road in Beaufort, open 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on weekdays. The county lists a $15 flat fee for a deed plus $1.85 per $500 of consideration, and a 0.25% Hilton Head Island transfer fee in certain district numbers. Confirm the current amounts with the office before closing.

The county requires original signatures, two witnesses, a notary statement, the District Map Parcel number, the buyer's address and a derivation clause. An Affidavit of True Consideration is needed when the price is not written on the face of the deed. E-recording partners include Simplifile and CSC Global, and documents received after 4:30 p.m. are processed the next business day.

sections.h2: What buyers check on an island house
sections.html:
Buyers of Hilton Head Island houses check a short list before they make an offer: the flood zone, the insurance quote, the HOA or association rules and any rental history. Sandy soil outside the tidal marsh and the island's low elevation make drainage and foundations worth a look. A house in a gated community also comes with entry rules, dues and sometimes architectural review, and a buyer will ask to see all three in writing.

Preparing those papers before listing keeps the deal moving. Put the association's rules and latest dues statement in one folder, along with the elevation certificate, the flood zone result and your permit history. If the house has been a rental, add the permit, the business license and the Local Accommodations Tax filings. A buyer who sees a complete file is far less likely to renegotiate.

Remember that second-home owners are often the likeliest sellers. If that is you, appoint someone local to meet the inspector, and decide who handles utilities, keys and the final walkthrough, since a missed handoff can delay the closing by days.

sections.h2: Selling for cash from a distance
sections.html:
A cash sale lets an island owner skip showings, the lender appraisal and the wait for a buyer who can qualify for a mortgage. The buyer looks at the property as it is, including any flood, roof or HOA issues, and you pick a closing date. Inherited homes, vacant second homes and houses with deferred maintenance are common here. You can turn an offer down at no cost.

If you live off the island, ask the closing attorney whether signing can be done by mail or at a local office, and who will hand over keys and gate access. Tell the association early, since many require notice, a fee or a transfer form at sale. Have your HOA dues statement and your insurance papers ready so nothing delays the closing.

faqs.q: Is Hilton Head Island its own town?
faqs.a: Yes. The Town of Hilton Head Island was incorporated after a May 1983 referendum. It sits in Beaufort County, which handles assessments, tax bills and deed recording.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Hilton Head Island house inside a gated community?
faqs.a: Yes. About 70% of the island lies inside gated communities, and each has an association with its own rules. Ask the association what a sale requires, such as notices or fees.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the 4% and 6% tax rate in Beaufort County?
faqs.a: The 4% ratio applies to a legal residence the owner lives in. Second homes and other real property are assessed at 6%. The legal residence application is due January 15, and a new owner must apply again.

faqs.q: Does my short-term rental permit transfer to a buyer?
faqs.a: The permit is issued to an individual, so contact the STR office at 843-341-4740 before you promise a buyer anything about rental income.

faqs.q: What flood records should I have ready to sell?
faqs.a: Have an elevation certificate, your flood zone from the Town's search tool and your permit history. The Town's Floodplain Administrator can help with certificates.
